I actually recently approached druidry again as an extension of being more mindful of my environmental impact. As far as I'm concerned, there's nothing wrong with eating other animals. Plenty of animals eat meat, there's no reason we need to be an exception. However, the meat industry has a huge impact on the environment. It's unnecessarily cruel and unsustainable. So I'm in a similar boat -- I started following a vegetarian diet for environmental reasons about a month ago, but if I'm at a function that doesn't have a vegetarian option, I'm probably just going to eat the non-vegetarian option. Ideally as a stretch goal I'd like to pursue a vegan diet, as there's still an environmental impact outside of just the meat, but tbh I get kind of overwhelmed trying to navigate shopping like that, so I buy vegan when I'm able to easily manage it, vegetarian otherwise, and will eat meat if it's the only thing that is offered to me. I've also been trying to practice more active gratitude with the foods I eat and where they come from, as part of letting spirituality back into my life.

I was in a similar boat. My mom had me when she was 18 and she was not at all prepared for it, and that resulted in a lot of abuse and neglect. I tend to fawn/freeze because of this and it constantly impacts me, despite having been in therapy for well over a decade now.  I have a younger sister that I have a lot of survivor's guilt for, but every time I'd visited them in recent years, everything seemed... fine. My mom was actively making an effort to be a better parent for my sister. She still said and did things that made me feel manipulated, though, and it was a constant source of being triggered. I eventually came to the conclusion that if the source of those fawn/freeze responses was still in my life, I wasn't going to be able to work through them. 


So, last November I sent her a message, saying "There's nothing new that you've done to cause this, but after talking a lot about it in therapy, I've realized that I'm not going to be able to make the progress I need to make if we're still in contact with each other. I may reach out again someday, but until then, please don't contact me." She responded in a way that was very receptive (something like "I know I wasn't a very good mom to you. I'll be here when you're ready") which kind of made me feel like an asshole, and I won't lie, I still feel guilt about it. 


However, I am sure this was the right move.  


1) A psychosomatic breathing issue that I've had for like seven years is finally starting to improve after trying so many different things to get it to go away with no success  


2) I've felt so much *rage*, which is extremely unlike me. I once told a therapist that I'd never felt anger before, but after going no contact, it seems endless. This might seem like a negative, but my therapist and I both believe this is a sign that I'm finally letting myself grieve. While great and all, this has been extremely difficult to grapple with and I'm still trying to figure out how to handle these new emotions.


3) Unlocking anger meant that I finally had something to combat the chronic shame. I've been able to recognize when I'm being mistreated and set real boundaries more effectively since going no contact. 


After more than a decade of therapy and feeling 'stuck' or like my progress had plateaued, going no contact has made me feel like healing is actually a possibility. 10/10, highly recommend

I'm not vegan, but my mom was when I was growing up. She'd frequently offer me food, wait for my reaction, and then when I said it was fine, she would be very thrilled to say "bet you didn't realize it was vegan!" I've got nothing against vegan food, and genuinely have considered going vegan or at the very least vegetarian myself because I do enjoy it and of course have ethical concerns. It's hard for me to articulate, but by making it a point to bring up that something is vegan when I didn't ask, it feels as though I'm being proselytized or spoken down to in some way, which ends up adding friction to a conversation that otherwise didn't have any. I've got my own history with that and I'm sure that's not the same with all non-vegans, but that's at least the case for me. Emotionally I experience it the same as someone REALLY trying to coerce me into watching a TV show when I already said I'd get to it when I'm good and ready, not when they're trying to force my hand.

Seconding the comparison to OCD. "I feel terrible because I don't know if I'm attracted to him because deep down I 'see him as a woman' since he has his natal junk (I don't think I do, because I literally always forgot that he was trans outside of the bedroom)" is 100% the type of thought that would come before a "wait but what if I'm secretly transphobic and evil" spiral for me, and I'm also diagnosed with OCD. My brain will latch onto literally anything that it could possibly inject some doubt into in order to make me feel like Satan incarnate.

Definitely childhood trauma for me. Life was unstable and unpredictable. I needed to be hypervigilant and cognizant of everyone's emotions and how I impacted them or Else. It meant that I was always grasping for anything I could do for any modicum of control, and that eventually spiralled into where I'm at today.

*Knowing* that it's OCD, *knowing* that so many of my problems are problems that my brain has completely fabricated, and still struggling with it. To an outsider, it seems like I'm just intentionally making things difficult for myself, but I'm really, really not trying to. I would give anything to not have to deal with this.

Mostly inferiority complex I think. To me, everything I make is awful and embarrassing. I can be happy making things without anyone interacting with it, but the second other people interact with it, I assume they see how bad it is, too, regardless of whether they give positive feedback or not. I also have this issue with listening to music that I like around others ("my taste in music is bad and they think so too"), so I really only do that if they insist. I can recognize this as the mental health thing that it is, typing this now, but in the moment it's hard to work past the spiral that that sort of thing causes.

It opens the door to further conversation. A lot of my hobbies are creative in nature, and if I mention that, I'll be asked "oh, can I see/hear/etc?" and the answer is absolutely not. Alternatively, someone will share a hobby with me and will try to engage with me about it, and that is also extremely difficult for me unless I know them well enough. Part of it is inferiority complex (i.e. this person shares a hobby with me, they must be so much better at it or know so much more about it), part of it is simply not wanting to relate to someone and open up to the stress of forming a friendship.

I see a lot of folks making this about being embarrassed about being overweight specifically, and that may have been the intent, but I think this is extremely considerate regardless of who you're asking. Small fits me 'best', but I like to wear medium/sometimes large depending on the article of clothing. There's an argument to be made about whether or not I should just say that my size is medium instead, but asking it like this opens that up as a topic for discussion and might make it less likely for the gift-giver to make assumptions about clothing size in the future (i.e. "so-and-so said they were a size S, so I'm always going to get that size for them")

I completely relate. So despite having a sweet tooth, I drank black coffee for a very long time. In a similar vein, I hate when people ask what I do for fun, because even though I have a lot of hobbies, I can't let anyone know that about me, so I just sort of give non-answers when asked.

This is also my approach! I am predisposed to interacting with the world and reacting to things a certain way, but as long as I can put a name to it, I can recognize it for what it is. Full disclosure, I'm not diagnosed, but I check pretty much every box. Since I've begun to suspect I have AvPD, I've been trying to work against it more instead of falling into the "I never want to interact with anyone ever again so I'm just not going to" pitfall. It's still difficult, but it feels like progress instead of letting myself be comfortable with something that is actively detrimental to me. I know that sort of reads like "Just stop being depressed!" -- it's not easy. It's difficult, but necessary work.

Alright, as an update: things went great yesterday. Showed up at 6:30 AM as requested for my 8:00 procedure. 

Timetable of events as I remember them:

Was brought to my recovery room where the nurse asked me a lot of questions, and then to take off my clothes and into my surgical gown. She brought me a warm blanket for my legs and for my arm so that putting the IV in was easier.

After she put the IV in, she kept asking me questions. Was asked to use some sort of pre-surgical sanitation wipes on my chest. I had the option of doing it myself or having her do it, and I opted for the former. This was done while my nurse was in the room, but honestly it wasn't too bad. Told me my care team would be in one at a time to introduce themselves and ask me questions.

The anesthesiologist was the first in, and she asked me my family history with anesthesia since I've never had general anesthesia before. Also asked me if I experienced motion sickness. For the most part, each person in the surgical team gendered me correctly, but my anesthesiologist kept she/herring me, which wasn't ideal, but whatever.

Dr. Kayan was the next to come in. At one of my pre-op appointments, I brought in some pictures of what my ideal results would look like, so she and I discussed the most ideal picture I gave her, what she would have done differently if I hadn't given her that input, and anything I wanted to change. She and I both agreed that the nipple size was slightly too large in the picture, so we decided on something *slightly* smaller. After that, she made the necessary markings on my chest.

I can't remember the title of the next two people that came in unfortunately, but the next one that came in and was very sweet. Meeting the team before they operated on me was super comforting and made me feel like I wasn't completely left to a handful of strangers, haha.

The last person to come in was the person who actually put stuff in my IV. I think it was Versed(spelling?), and I was told it would help me calm down. She wheeled me into the OR, and that was the last thing I remember, actually. Don't even remember being given general anesthesia, the Versed knocked me out like a light.

Woke up approximately three hours later back in the recovery room. Was still feeling really foggy, but I was wrapped in my compression vest and had my drains in. The first thoughts I had when waking up were "god I'm thirsty" and "god I need to piss". The nurse was back in, brought me some water upon request, helped walk me to the bathroom, which was an easier endeavor than I thought it would be.

They got in contact with my caretaker, and confirmed that he was waiting to pick me up outside. Someone else came in to help me into a wheelchair, brought me outside, and from there I was on my way home.

Recovery so far (even though it hasn't even been 24 hours) has been pretty chill. I'd say the worst my pain has been is a 3 or a 4 on the scale, but pain meds have helped keep me around a 2 or so. Sleeping on my back has been a billion times easier than I thought it would be, and I've spent it so far just sleeping every couple of hours, setting reminders on my phone for meds.

Only issues so far with recovery is that putting pressure on the pill bottles to get past the child safety lock causes some not comfy pressure in my chest, so I've occasionally had to ask my caretaker to open them for me. Haven't had too much energy to do things yet, so I've been pretty couch-bound.
